lessons.title: Graph Terminology and Types
lessons.concept: A graph consists of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections). Graphs can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and cyclic or acyclic. Degree, path, and connectivity are basic properties used to describe graphs.
lessons.formula: Graph G = (V, E). Undirected edge {u,v}; directed edge (u,v). In undirected graph, degree is number of incident edges.
lessons.worked_example: Vertices {A,B,C} with edges {A-B, B-C} form an undirected path graph. A points to B, B to C in a directed version.
mistakes: Treating a path as a cycle without returning to start appropriately
Miscounting degree in directed graphs (in-degree vs out-degree)
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Graph Representations
lessons.concept: Graphs are commonly represented using adjacency matrices or adjacency lists. Adjacency matrix uses a VxV table to mark edges; adjacency list stores neighbors for each vertex. Choice depends on graph density and operations.
lessons.formula: Adjacency matrix: matrix[u][v]=1 (or weight) if edge exists. Adjacency list: for each u store list of adjacent vertices v.
lessons.worked_example: For edges A-B, A-C in undirected graph, adjacency list: A:[B,C], B:[A], C:[A]. Matrix has 1s at (A,B),(B,A),(A,C),(C,A).
mistakes: Using matrix for very sparse large graphs without considering memory (O(V^2))
Forgetting to add both directions for undirected graphs in adjacency list/matrix
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: BFS and DFS Introduction
lessons.concept: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores neighbors level by level using a queue, useful for shortest path in unweighted graphs. Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as deep as possible before backtracking using recursion or a stack.
lessons.formula: BFS: enqueue start, mark visited, while queue not empty dequeue and enqueue unvisited neighbors. DFS: visit node, recursively/stack-visit unvisited neighbors.
lessons.worked_example: From A connected to B,C and B connected to D: BFS order from A can be A,B,C,D (level-wise). DFS order can be A,B,D,C (depth-first).
mistakes: Not marking nodes visited, causing infinite loops in cyclic graphs
Using stack logic mentally but implementing queue (or vice versa)
Assuming BFS/DFS give same traversal order

practice.explanation: An adjacency matrix is a V x V table, requiring O(V^2) space regardless of the number of edges.

questions.question: For a sparse graph with many vertices but few edges, which representation is usually more space-efficient?
questions.explanation: Adjacency lists store only existing edges/neighbors (O(V+E) space), which is more efficient than an adjacency matrix (O(V^2)) for sparse graphs.

questions.question: BFS is commonly used to find the shortest path (in number of edges) in which type of graph?

options.B: Any negatively weighted graph without changes

questions.explanation: BFS explores vertices in increasing order of edge distance from the source, so it finds shortest paths in terms of fewest edges in unweighted graphs.

questions.question: Why is a visited set/array important in BFS/DFS on graphs that may contain cycles?

options.B: To avoid revisiting nodes and infinite loops
options.C: To convert graph to tree automatically

questions.explanation: In graphs with cycles, without tracking visited nodes the traversal can revisit the same vertices repeatedly, leading to infinite loops or redundant work.
